en: The Buddha’s teachings were led westward from India, and the sutras and śāstras were translated eastward to China; one should know that this was due to great causes and conditions, and did not arise without reason.

The Prajñāpāramitā relied upon Master Xuanzang for its propagation, while the Avataṃsaka-sūtra depended upon Master Xianshou for its elucidation. As for the Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī Sūtra, it is not merely a literary work.
It was not possible for any other great sage to initiate it; it was not possible for anyone other than the Venerable Pārśva to request its translation.
Master Dingjue has already provided a detailed account of this. During the reign of the Qing Dynasty, the venerable master Zhang of Yunqi [resided] within the Zunsengdang Hall of Xiangfu Temple.
This dhāraṇī sūtra was recorded, and although efforts were made to commission its carving, it remained unfinished. Recently, Zhang Kaishi, a local lay practitioner, suddenly beheld a wondrous light.
On the first day of the seventh month, he came to me to resolve his doubts; I urged him to quickly print and distribute it so that it might spread widely. As an ancient virtuous master’s verse says:
The Venerable Póli paid homage at Mount Wú-tái, where he was transformed by Mañjuśrī, who said:

"If the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī* did not exist in this eastern land, it would be difficult for sentient beings to escape the dust of the mundane world. Thus, one knows that the dhāraṇī sūtras are of great benefit to the world and to future generations.

After I had lectured on the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, I concurrently translated chapters of dhāraṇīs from the Esoteric Section; upon carefully examining the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā*, both its earlier and later versions...
Ten translations: 1. In the first year of the Yifeng era of the Tang dynasty, the Venerable Póli (Bhāṣita) first came to court to pay homage at Mount Wutai.

In the fourth year of Yifeng, he took the scriptures and returned to the Western Capital (Chang’an), where he translated them. 2. In the first year of the Tiàolù era, Bhāṣita and Du Xingyi, Court Disperser, translated them together.
3. In the first year of the Yongchun era, by imperial decree, the Tripiṭaka Master Rìzhào (Dharmarakṣa) was ordered to translate them together with Du Xingyi.
In the first year of the Guangzhai era, Pali and Shunzheng jointly translated it (4).
In the third year of the Chuihong era, Zhijing and the Tripiṭaka Master Rizi translated it (5). Although this scripture was translated five times in succession, it is but a single sūtra.
It concerns how, upon the death of the Devaputra Sunirmita after seven days, he entreated Śakra to pay homage to the Buddha, who then emitted light for his sake.
6. This mantra was translated by the Tang Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra as the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-paṭala-vidhi*;
it is simply the mantra from the fifth of the aforementioned [texts]. 7. The Song Tripiṭaka Master Dharmadeva translated the *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Most Victorious Buddha-uṣṇīṣa*;
however, the text contains no prose commentary on the mantra. 8. The Song Tripiṭaka Master Dharmadeva retranslated it, titled *The Buddha-Spoken Dhāraṇī of the Uṣṇīṣa of All Tathāgatas*.
The *Sarva-sāra-parama-dhāraṇī-sūtra* contains both the prose and the mantra. However, the mantra sections in these two versions are twice as long as those in the Chinese translation.
This is because Śākyamuni Buddha, while in the Hall of Good Dharma (*Saddharma-hall*) in Sukhāvatī, spoke it for the sake of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Ninth, the Guru Acala refined this and incorporated it into the ritual procedures for the *bali* offering (*piṇḍapātra-vidhi*). Tenth, Mingren...
Empress Xiaokao dreamed that she was moved by the Buddha’s preaching of the *Sutra on the Most Rare and Wondrous Merits*.

Of the six previous translations, the first six were for lifting those in the six realms of existence out of the three miserable paths; the latter four were for guiding those of the four modes of birth to ascend through the nine grades of rebirth.
In sum, this mantra is the very foundation for being born in the heavens and pure lands. That which is currently practiced is the fourth translation from the Tang dynasty, according to the sutra.

To speak thus brings great benefit to the Dharma. By reciting and contemplating it day and night, one attains the eight supreme fruits; by offering incense, flowers, and worship, one possesses the fourfold renown.
For those suffering from illness, it eliminates disease and calamity; for those with short lifespans, it increases their heavenly years; and for those who enjoy meager merit, [it brings abundance].
One may now enjoy its benefits. Those of the most evil destiny shall escape the three miserable realms; birds and beasts who hear its sound shall never again fall [into such states];
even those touched by its wind or shadow shall realize Great Bodhi. Writing it once or upholding it once brings about the two benefits in the virtuous paths;

remembering it once or hearing it once gains ten advantages from the Buddhas and devas. With such manifest verification, it is specifically circulated for the sake of others, just as in the case of the One [Vehicle].
From within the treasury of jewels, he takes forth inexhaustible wish-fulfilling gems and distributes them as gifts to all sentient beings of the world and future generations.
One should know with faith that the Bodhisattva has accomplished the most supreme and rare dharmas in the world; truly, there is a great causal connection here.
All who see, hear, or rejoice in this should follow and practice according to the teaching.
Record of the Circumstances of the Discourse by the Śramaṇa Xufa of Ciyun Monastery at Donglin,
Hangzhou, Zhejiang, on the Birthday of the Sixth Xin Cycle, the Eleventh Day of the Tenth Month in the Gengchen Year of the Kangxi Reign.

The *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra* was spoken by Śakra Devendra for the sake of the divine son Sudhāna, who had fallen into the realm of animals seven times and sought the Buddha’s compassionate salvation.
During the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, the Western monk Pāli traveled to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī and personally received the holy entrustment.
Upon returning to his own country, he requested its transmission; it was not until the third year of the Chuixiong era that it was finally translated and disseminated. [Song]...

After the Yuan dynasty, it was preserved within the Imperial Treasury. At the beginning of our present dynasty, the monk Guangzhang of Yunqi passed through Xiangfu and beheld this scripture and mantra offered atop a jeweled banner;
overcome with joy and praise, he burned incense and transcribed it. He once solicited funds for its carving, which I have now undertaken.

Due to being bound by worldly affairs, the carving and printing were not completed. Now, on the waning moon following the full moon of the sixth month, while reciting scriptures in my ear-chamber, I suddenly heard a thunderous sound.
Rising from my seat and hurrying to look, I saw a flash of lightning-like light within the doorway. For several days, I was filled with alarm and doubt.
Then, in the midst of a dream, I recalled an old monk from the past who lived in seclusion deep in the mountains, reciting the Lotus Sūtra every day for several decades.
He did not cease his work through cold or heat. Because the original manuscript of the scripture was damaged, he sent it to Zhaokong Temple for repair.

While the eunuch Sun Longgong was staying overnight at a villa by the lake, he walked out under the moonlight toward the scripture room; there, a beam of light shot forth. Upon knocking and inquiring, the place was silent and devoid of anyone.
He was perplexed by this anomaly and could not understand it. The next morning, he consulted the monk for a resolution.

The monk replied, "I have done nothing more than repair a single copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* from its old state; I possess no other objects. When the official went to visit him, the monk informed his disciples one day prior:
"Tomorrow morning, someone will come seeking me to inquire about my past and present traces. Wait until the day the river is dredged, and I shall return. Thus he spoke.

Having finished, he bathed and sat in meditation before passing away. In the year of Kāngxī Jiǎzǐ, when the river was opened, the Provincial Governor Zhao, whose name was Shìlín, was none other than this monk returned once more.
Is this present manifestation of light perhaps the same? I immediately searched through my collection of scriptures and found a copy of the *Guǎngshèng zūnshèng jì*.
Without realizing it, I was struck with awe and trepidation; could this not be our Buddha, urgently desiring to deliver us?

"Is it because of the suffering of sentient beings that these extraordinary signs have appeared? He then requested the Dharma Master Boting of Ciyun Temple to examine the Tripitaka for verification and provide a phonetic commentary.
Suddenly, a friend delivered a sacred image of Mañjuśrī to his home. His reverence and admiration redoubled, and he vowed to gild the image and offer worship to it morning and evening.
One should know that my being able to behold the countenance of the Sage today is due to this.

It must be that the venerable patriarch Pāli of old encountered a transformation body and received this entrustment. I have therefore requested that it be transcribed and carved into woodblocks, so that it may be swiftly printed and distributed.
May all people of future generations throughout the world emerge from the seven destinies into the Three Vehicles and transcend the four modes of birth within the Ten Stages.
May those who see or hear it have their past karma entirely extinguished and attain a pure body through its recitation.
This eliminates the sufferings of the three miserable realms and leads one into the lands of all Buddhas. As for these causes and effects, how could they be fathomed by the ordinary mind?
Therefore, I have recorded these preceding and subsequent circumstances to propagate them widely.
Written on the morning of the full moon of the ninth month in the year of Gengchen, the thirty-ninth year of the Kangxi reign,
by Zhang Shihun Zoping of Wulin, having bathed and purified himself.
Preface to the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī Sūtra*, composed by the śramaṇa Zhijing of Dingjue Monastery.
Regarding the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī Sūtra*: it was [brought by] the Brahman monk Buddhapālita during the first year of the Yifeng era.
In the [blank] year, he came from the Western Regions to this land. Upon reaching Mount Wutai, he prostrated himself fully on the ground and paid homage toward the mountain peak, saying:
"Since the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the various sages have remained hidden in their spiritual power;

only the Great Being Mañjuśrī remains here within these mountains to draw forth the common people and instruct the Bodhisattvas. My only regret is that I was born at a time beset by the eight difficulties."

Having beheld the Holy Countenance, I have traveled far across the shifting sands to come here in reverent audience. I beseech you, Greatly Compassionate and Most Merciful One, to extend your universal protection so that I may behold your venerable form.

Having spoken, he wept with tears falling like rain and prostrated himself toward the mountain. Upon rising from his prostration and looking up, he suddenly saw an old man emerge from within the mountains.
The man addressed the monk in the language of the Brahmins, saying: "The Dharma Master’s heart is set upon..."
Devoted to the Way, he pursued the traces of the Sage, undaunted by toil and hardship as he sought out distant ruins.
However, the sentient beings of the land of Han frequently commit sinful deeds, and even those who have left the household life often violate the precepts.

Only the *Buddhottamasikhātilaka-dhāraṇī-sūtra* can extinguish and eliminate such evil karma. He did not know whether the Dharma Master had perhaps brought this sutra with him. The monk replied, "I am poor..."
Daozhi came directly to pay his respects, but did not bring the scriptures with him. The old man said, "Since you have not brought the scriptures, what is the benefit of coming empty-handed?
Even if you were to see Mañjuśrī, why would you necessarily recognize him? You should instead return to the Western Land to fetch these scriptures and bring them to China.

By circulating them throughout the land of Han, you will be universally honoring all the sages, extensively benefiting all living beings, rescuing those in both the netherworld and the world of light, and repaying the kindness of all the Buddhas."
The Master took the scripture and arrived here. "Disciple, I shall show you where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī resides.
Upon hearing these words, the monk was overcome with joy; he checked his tears and paid homage with a sincere heart.
In the brief moment it took him to raise his head, the old man suddenly vanished. Startled and amazed, the monk redoubled his devotion and, with focused mindfulness and utmost sincerity, turned back.

In the Western Regions, [the Emperor] obtained the *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. In the second year of the Yongchun era, he returned to the Western Capital (Xi'jing) and reported the aforementioned matters in detail to the Great Emperor.

The Great Emperor then took the original manuscript into the palace and invited the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman (Rìzhào), along with Du Xingyi, the Director of Guest Relations at the Department of State Ceremonies, and others to jointly translate this sūtra by imperial decree. The edict stated:
He bestowed thirty rolls of silk upon the Sangha; however, the original scripture was kept within and not brought out. The monk wept bitterly and submitted this petition:

"This humble monk has risked his body and surrendered his life to travel afar to fetch this scripture. My heartfelt hope is to universally save all living beings and deliver them from suffering and hardship."

He did not set his mind on wealth or treasure, nor did he concern himself with fame or profit. He requested that the translated scriptures be circulated so that all sentient beings might share in the benefit.
The Emperor then retained the translated scriptures and returned the Sanskrit manuscripts to the monk. Having received the Sanskrit manuscripts, the monk...
He was about to go to Ximing Monastery to seek out the Chinese monk Shunzheng, who was proficient in Sanskrit, to petition the Emperor to translate [the texts] together with him.

The Emperor granted his request. The monk then, in the presence of the great virtuous ones, translated together with Shunzheng. Once the translation was complete, the monk took the Sanskrit manuscripts.
He headed toward Mount Wutai; having entered the mountains, he has not emerged until this day. I have now translated two versions, both of which circulate in the world.
Should there be minor discrepancies in the phrasing, I hope you will not find them strange.

In the third year of the Chuigong era, the abbot of Dingjue Monastery, the monk Zhijing, while staying at the Wei-guo Dongsi Temple in the Divine Capital (Luoyang), personally encountered the Dharma Master Tripitaka Sūryavarman.
The Master questioned him regarding his delay, and he related everything exactly as previously stated. Zhijing then approached the Tripiṭaka Master to inquire about and receive the divine mantras.

Thereupon, the Dharma Master orally transmitted the Sanskrit text; after two weeks, he had bestowed every sentence in detail, ensuring that the Sanskrit pronunciation was complete and without a single error.
He further compared this with the existing Sanskrit manuscripts used for previous translations, and all omissions or mistakes were completely corrected.

Revised. Regarding the initial note to this mantra stating that "the final version is a separate translation," it is indeed so. The phrasing of this mantra differs slightly from that translated by Du Ling.
This new mantra has been revised and corrected without error; its phonetic transcriptions have also been completed. May future scholars examine this in detail.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Yongchang era, at Dajing’ai Temple, [I] saw the Ximing...
At the temple, the Elder Dharma Master Cheng inquired about his stay, and he replied as previously stated. The translation monk Shunzheng was seen at Ximing Temple.
This scripture provides salvation for those in both the hidden and manifest realms and is most inconceivable;
fearing that students might not understand it, I have recorded its details in full to transmit it to those who have not yet awakened.
Homage to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha (recite three times).
Verse for Opening the Sutra:
The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma, Difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.
I have now seen, heard, and received this for upholding; may I understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
*Commentary on the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, translated from the Northern and Southern Canons.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Buddhāpālita of Jibin during the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of great bodhisattvas.
Together with twelve thousand people.
At that time, in the assembly hall of the Sudharmā Hall in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there was a son of heaven named Sunetra (Good Abiding).
He was wandering through the gardens and groves with the great devas, enjoying supreme nobility alongside them, and was preceded by various celestial maidens.
Thereafter, they surrounded him, joyfully sporting and delighting together with various kinds of music, experiencing every pleasure.
At that time, during the night, the Devaputra Susthita heard a voice say: "Devaputra Susthita, seven days from now your life will come to an end.
After your death, you shall be born in Jambudvīpa and undergo the bodies of animals for seven successive rebirths. Immediately—
They undergo the sufferings of hell. Emerging from hell, they rarely obtain a human body; even when born, they are impoverished and lowly.
While dwelling in the mother’s womb, they are immediately born without both eyes. At that time, having heard these sounds, the Devaputra Sunetra was struck with great terror;
his hair stood on end, and he was filled with grief and distress. He hurried to the abode of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, where he wailed and wept in trembling fear.
Without hesitation, he prostrated at the feet of Śakra, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings, and addressed Śakra, saying:
"Listen to what I have to say. While I was enjoying various pleasures, surrounded by celestial maidens, I heard a voice declare:
'Good Dwelling Devaputra, seven days from now your life will come to an end; after your death, you will be reborn in Jambudvīpa and undergo the state of an animal for seven successive lifetimes.'"
Having received these seven bodies, I immediately fell into the various hells. Emerging from hell, I rarely obtained a human body;
when born into a poor and lowly family, I was blind in both eyes. O Lord of Devas, how may I be delivered from this suffering?
At that time, having heard the words of the devaputra Susīma, Śakra was greatly astonished. He then reflected to himself:
"What seven rebirths in the evil destinies has this devaputra Susīma undergone? Thereupon, Śakra remained in quietude for a moment.
Entering meditative concentration and observing with discernment, he saw that Sudṛśa was destined to undergo seven more births in the miserable realms—
namely, as a pig, a dog, a jackal, a monkey, a python, a crow, and a vulture— consuming various foul, evil, and impure things. At that time, Śakra,
seeing that the devaputra Sudṛśa was about to fall into seven successive births in the miserable realms, felt extreme compassion for his suffering.

This pierced his heart with pain. Reflecting deeply, he found no way out; to whom could he turn for refuge? There was only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who could cause him to dwell securely and enable him to escape this suffering.
At that time, during the first watch of this very night, Śakra, adorned with various flower garlands, unguents, and powdered incense,
and carrying exquisite celestial robes, went to the Jeta Grove. Having arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was,
he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and made vast offerings before the Buddha, standing with his feet planted before him.
Kneeling, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why will the devaputra Sunihita receive the body of an animal seven times in the evil realms of rebirth?
He related everything as previously described.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted various kinds of light from the crown of his head, which filled all worlds throughout the ten directions.
The light then returned, circled the Buddha three times, and entered through his mouth. The Buddha then smiled and addressed Śakra, saying:
"Devendra, there is a dhāraṇī called the 'Exalted and Victorious Uṣṇīṣa of the Tathāgata. It is able to purify all evil realms and..."
It completely purifies all the sufferings and afflictions of birth and death. It can also purify the sufferings of the various hells, the realm of King Yama, and the animal kingdom.
Furthermore, it shatters all hells and enables one to dedicate merit toward the auspicious paths.
O Lord of Devas, if there is anyone who hears this Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī, even once passing through their ears, all the [karmic consequences] of the hells created in previous lives—
All evil karma shall be completely extinguished, and one shall obtain a pure body. Wherever one is born, one shall remember and not forget.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, from one celestial realm to another celestial realm, one shall travel throughout the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
in every place of birth, one shall remember and not forget. O Lord of Devas, if a person’s life is about to end, in a mere moment—
By recollecting this dhāraṇī, one shall regain increased longevity, attain purity of body, speech, and mind, and be free from physical suffering.
According to its merit and benefit, one shall find peace and security in every place. One will be beheld by all Tathāgatas and constantly guarded by all celestial deities.
Honored by people, one’s evil obstructions shall be eliminated, and all Bodhisattvas will protect one with a single heart. O Deva...

O Emperor, if there is a person who can read and recite this dhāraṇī for even a brief moment, all the sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, the realm of King Yama, and the hungry ghosts belonging to that person shall be shattered and extinguished, leaving nothing behind.
They will encounter no obstacles in entering the Buddha-fields, the celestial palaces of the various devas, or the gateways where all bodhisattvas dwell. Following...

As his mind entered into this state, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of sentient beings, expound the Dharma for increasing the span of life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts and intentions in the mind of Śakra, [perceived] his desire to hear the Buddha preach this.
The Dharani Method. He then spoke the mantra, saying (this mantra is translated separately at the end): Namaḥ bhagavate tiryag-loka-prati-viśiṣṭāya buddhāya.
(I) Homage to the Holy Honored One, the Victorious Awakened One of the Three Times. (II) Bhagavati.
(III) Tadyathā. (IV) Oṃ. (V) Viśuddha-ya-samantabhasa. (VI) Parabrahma-gahana. (VII) Bhasmabhūṣita-abhiṣeka-svāhā.

Śrī-ṣṭi (22) vi-sa-pu-ṭha-buddhi-ṣṭi (23) śaye śaye (24) viśaye viśaye (25) sam-ra-sam-ra-buddhā-deścitā-ṣṭi (26) vajra-ga-ḍa.

The Buddha addressed Śakra, saying: "This mantra is named the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*, which Purifies All Evil Realms.
It can eliminate all obstacles such as sinful karma and can shatter all suffering within the defiled evil realms.
O Lord of Devas, this dhāraṇī was proclaimed together by eighty-eight hundred-thousand-koṭi-gaṅgā-sand numbers of Buddhas. Following...
I joyfully accept and uphold this. It is sealed with the Great Tathāgata’s Wisdom Seal. This is for the sake of destroying the suffering of the evil realms of all sentient beings;
for the sake of bringing liberation to all beings in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of King Yama;

and for the sake of bringing liberation to those sentient beings who, facing urgent hardships and perils, have fallen into the ocean of birth and death, and who possess short lifespans, meager merit, and no protection.
This is taught for the sake of sentient beings who delight in creating various defiled and evil karmas. Furthermore, by the power of sustaining this *dhāraṇī* within Jambudvīpa,
it enables sentient beings in the hells and evil realms, those wandering through various births and deaths with meager merit,
and those who lack faith in the causality of good and evil deeds and have lost the right path, to attain the meaning of liberation.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: "I have spoken this dhāraṇī and entrust it to you.
You should bestow it upon the Devaputra Susthitamati, and you yourself should likewise uphold, recite, contemplate with joy, keep in mind, and make offerings to it.
Furthermore, you should widely proclaim this dhāraṇī for the sake of all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, and also for the sake of all the devaputras."
I have spoken this dhāraṇī-seal and entrust it to you, Devendra. You should maintain and protect it well; do not let it be forgotten or lost.
Devendra, if anyone should hear this dhāraṇī for even a moment, [the evil karma] accumulated over a thousand kalpas will be exhausted.
Heavy obstructions. One shall undergo various transmigrations through birth and death, receiving the bodies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, the realm of King Yama, and asuras;
as well as yakṣas, rākṣasas, spirits, bhūtas, kaṭapūtanas, apasmāras, mosquitoes, gadflies, tortoises, dogs, pythons, snakes, all kinds of birds, and all predatory beasts—every crawling creature.
All sentient beings, even those as small as ants, shall never again undergo further rebirth;

they will immediately attain rebirth in the assembly of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before Buddhahood, or they will be born into families of great nobility or Brahmins.
Or they may be born into a family of great kṣatriyas, or born into a most eminent and noble family.
O Lord of Devas, that these persons obtain such high and noble births as described above is entirely due to hearing this dhāraṇī, which transforms the place of their rebirth.
All shall attain purity, O Lord of Devas; even until they reach the most supreme place of the bodhi-maṇḍala, it is all due to the merit of praising this dhāraṇī in such a manner.
"O Lord of Devas, this dhāraṇī is named 'Auspicious. It can purify all evil realms.

This Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī is like a sun-treasury maṇi jewel: pure and free from blemish, its purity equal to space, its radiant flames penetrating and illuminating everywhere without exception. If sentient beings uphold this dhāraṇī, they shall likewise be so."
It is also like Jāmbūnada gold—luminous, pure, supple, and pleasing to behold—and cannot be defiled by impurities.
O Lord of Devas, if there are sentient beings who uphold this dhāraṇī, they shall likewise be thus:
by means of this virtuous purity, they will attain birth in the good realms. O Lord of Devas, wherever this dhāraṇī may be found, if one can transcribe and circulate it...
If one can thus master, uphold, recite, hear, and make offerings to it, all evil realms will become purified,
and all the sufferings of hell will be completely extinguished.

The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: "If there are those who can transcribe this dhāraṇī and place it atop a high banner, or on a high mountain, or upon a multi-storied pavilion, or even install it within a stūpa;
and if, Śakra, there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or sons and daughters of noble family who see it upon such banners or other locations..."
Or they may come into close proximity such that its shadow falls upon their bodies; or wind may blow dust from the banners atop Mount Dhāraṇī onto their persons.

O Lord of Devas, all those sentient beings shall not experience any of the karmic offenses that would otherwise cause them to fall into the miserable realms—the suffering of the hells, the animal realm, the world of Yama, the hungry ghosts, or the asuras. Nor shall they suffer these miseries.
They are not defiled by the stains of sin. O Lord of Devas, these sentient beings have received the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas;
